utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I need to remind you what Judge Richard May was already mentioned, who, for professional reasons which have to do with the work of the Tribunal, will not be here today. My colleague, Judge Robinson, and myself will be sitting today. I think there are no objections, so Ms. Somers, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There was no English translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: There was no English?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Is there a problem with the interpreters in the English booth?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No. One, two, three. I think the channels got mixed up. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Somers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Of course, just for the record, there's absolutely no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you now getting the interpretation into English?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Thank you. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, yesterday we left off with my indicating that I would, as per plan, work backward a little bit from 1993 to the events in 1992. I would like to ask you a little bit, though, if you can tell me, about your role, as you had indicated, as a substitute for the priest. What were the circumstances under which you had to assume the role of, as it were, substitute priest for the Serbian Orthodox community?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The priest who worked in Busovaca had problems because he had to service two parishes. He was also attacked in Zenica so he left that area. He escaped to Serbia where he was born, and he continued to work there. The priest who worked in Zenica authorised me to exercise the duties of a priest there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What duties did you, in fact, exercise? Were they religious duties or communal duties in relation to the members of the Serb community and, let's say, the central government, or what?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were only religious duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Serbian Orthodox Church was a focal point, was it not, of the community, the Serbian community?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The premises of -- the facilities of the Serbian Orthodox Church were only used by the Dobrotvor organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which had a function of distribution of humanitarian aid, as you indicated yesterday; that is correct?.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is where the distribution of humanitarian aid was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which, to a great measure, depended on the relationships between the conflicting parties and the International Community; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't feel that because it had been -- these things were organised. We had no conflicts with either side. We received our rations regularly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. The receipt of those rations, however, depended on their getting through, which was -- the getting through aspect is what I'm trying to emphasise. That depended on the International Community, did it not, the ability to pass by roads and go from territory to territory. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask a little bit about the relationships between and among the three ethnic groups, the Muslims, the Croats, and the Serbs, up to mid-1992, let's say up to about the 10th of May, 1992. The first part of the question is directed toward how the war that was going on between Serbia and Croatia affected the communities, and then if you could maybe move into how the war which then moved into the Mostar area between the Serbs and the non-Serb residents of Mostar affected the relationships. Please tell us a bit about that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing to say about that. I never engaged in politics and I wasn't involved in any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The question involves Mostar. I believe the city of Mostar, Your Honour, was not addressed at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat that because we were not getting the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Sorry. I was a little bit late leaping to my feet. It appears that this question addresses circumstances in Mostar, and that's something that certainly was not covered at any point, even inferentially, in direct examination and therefore is completely outside the scope of the direct examination, and I objected for that reason. It's also irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honours? Will the Court give me permission to respond as to why I'm asking this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, all the relationships, as we have consistently tried to show, between and among ethnic groups are not dependent solely on what is occurring simply in Central Bosnia. This indictment is premised upon the concept of widespread and systematic. The relationships which are described and the activities which are described in the case in chief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Could you move on rather rapidly. You have just asked a question which is very long.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There was no English, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: No English? Okay. I'll try to speak in English at this time. Can you please ask a precise question, because your question was very long. About the ethnic relationships, I think there were two parts. Ask your two questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, I'll break them down, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, as you indicated, you were a small number of persons in Busovaca municipality, relatively speaking. Can you talk about the relationships that may or may not have changed between and among the groups as a result of the war between Serbia and Croatia from 1991. I do not ask you necessarily as a political person; I ask you, as you called yourself in your summary, as a private person. How were the relationships affected, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a politician, I cannot tell you, because I was not into politics and I don't know. And as for the relations, they did not change much in that part.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did the Serb community feel that it had to be more cautious because it belonged to a group which was, certainly technically, of the same nationality as what has been described as the aggressor? Did that cause, let's say, hesitation among the members of the Serb community?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The second part of my question concerned the relationships that may or may not have been affected by the moving of the conflict into Bosnia, where troops backed by the JNA began attacks on non-Serb communities in Mostar, on the territory of the same country in which you were living. Did that make any difference or cause any extra concern among those in the Serb communities -- community, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Busovaca, where we were living, we did not feel any change. Nobody harassed us to begin to feel ill at ease, out of place there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were aware --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers. Mr. Bilic, the question that was asked of you was the following: Did you yourself at some point feel perhaps some hostility or suspicion or mistrust between the ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not feel any of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, I'm going to ask you just to look at something and ask for your reaction to it and how it may have affected your community.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I could ask for Z46.2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, the same objection under Rule 90(h). I think the Rule is absolutely clear. The cross-examination shall be limited to the subject matter of the direct examination or matters affecting credibility. But of course, the Trial Chamber has discretion to permit inquiry into additional matters, although it has to be conducted as if on direct examination. But the point is this: It is completely beyond the scope of anything that we covered with the witness on direct examination, and completely irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, I think that the Rule has very well been stated. Yesterday it was clearly spelled out by the President, and you were here, which is that we will maintain -- we will stick to what has been said in direct examination, apart from, obviously, the questions that have to deal with credibility. But I do not see in which way this letter is linked to what we -- the issue we're dealing with here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may -- I'm sorry. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think this is a very important point, and I want to indicate to the Court that I will tie this in. One of the fundamental issues in this case is what was going on between the Serbs and the Croats. It is an essential issue that must be documented to the Court, as well as through live testimony. The fact that a witness was not political does not mean, of course, that he or his community is not affected by the political things happening around him. In fact, the statements that were given on direct examination suggest a willful blindness to circumstances that are obvious, and I must bring this to the Court's attention about what was happening, that any Serb community that was concerned, rightfully, about its own relationships should have been aware of. And the points that are in the next -- I have about seven documents, and no more, I think are critical at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, I think that these questions -- we did have other opportunities to deal with them in this Trial Chamber. I think that you should now go on to a different question. I really cannot see the relation with this witness. You asked him questions about inter-ethnic relations. He said that nothing happened. So the Trial Chamber will draw the consequences from that, and please proceed with another line of questioning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: All right. I will reserve some of these critical documents for next week's witnesses. Thank you. And perhaps Mr. Nice will be able to avail himself of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you if you had become aware, as a member of the Serb community, about certain changes occurring between the political leadership, not yourself, of the Serbs generally in Bosnia and the political leadership of the Croats in Bosnia. Did you know about those changes in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever changes there were, I was aware of some of them, but I did not engage in politics and I didn't go into that area. All we wanted was to protect ourselves, to survive, and we did not want to meddle into any political processes or political events; we just wanted to survive in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I see. Then you are suggesting that you were unaware of a ceasefire agreement that was signed between Radovan Karadzic and Mate Boban at the very end of April, approximately 27 April 1992, in Graz, Austria, which was announced publicly by all means of communication -- radio, print media, other electronic media -- on 6 May 1992. Are you saying that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honour. Once again, that was not covered in direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers, I believe you have to stop interrupting us. We have other concerns. Ms. Somers is verifying the credibility of the witness by this question, and she is fully entitled to ask you, because she's asking -- she should be allowed to ask the question. It is simply a factor of adjudicated facts and so she's completely in her right to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bilic, would you please answer the question?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already stated, and I can repeat it a hundred times: I did not engage in politics and I didn't hear about it. I could have heard about it, but I wasn't engaging in those things. I just wasn't involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, I think that you should now change the subject. We have come to the end of this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a little bit about your initial comments on the changes that took place in Busovaca after what you called a supposed change in government, but which many other witnesses have called a putsch or a coup. Can I ask you, please, when after the 10th of May 1992 did you first go back into the town of Busovaca from your home near Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I would go there occasionally. I said that I did go to Busovaca occasionally. But I did not write down the exact dates when I went there or when I came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When did you -- did you have to continue your work with Dobrotvor to keep humanitarian aid collected and distributed during the time or shortly after the change in the government?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The food was distributed once or twice a month, and that's when I went to town. And as far as the distribution of food was concerned, there were no changes; that is, the food was distributed and it went on being distributed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But it was kept in the church, is that correct, in the centre of the town?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The church is not in the centre of town; it is at the outskirts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Within the municipality, within the town of Busovaca, though? When you say "outskirts," it's still town of Busovaca as opposed to your hamlet or somewhere on the road to your hamlet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very entrance to town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you indicated that you were terribly concerned about a crime problem. Who was protecting the stores of food? Who would check up to make sure there was no pillaging of your supplies? Did you have to do that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because the food was in the central warehouse. The central warehouse had security. The UNPROFOR provided it. And then UNPROFOR would notify us, we would come and pick up the food that same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you recall, between the 10th of May and the 22nd of May, going into the town of Busovaca for any purpose?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Serb police officers who you said did not change their positions after the change of government, can you please give us their names?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of them still lives in Busovaca. He is retired. His name is Milenko Hercegovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And was he in Busovaca during the entire period of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether or not he had a weapon which he took home?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you notice when you got back into the town of Busovaca after the 10th of May, 1992, that a Croat flag was flying over the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you something. When I went to town, when I went to the church, I could go there five or six times to go to the Dobrotvor and never to go downtown.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And no one with whom you associated, including the Serb police officers who must have had to go into town, told you that a Croat flag was then flying over the municipal building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not socialise with the Serbian policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was anyone you know affected by the total blockade around Busovaca that was put in place by an order of Dario Kordic on the 10th of May, 1992, and lifted by the same persons on the 22nd of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of anyone having had any problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Does your house have electricity?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you own a television?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you own a radio -- did you own a radio and television at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you ever listen to or watch those two media?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally I watched television.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated that you met with Dario Kordic, apparently for the first time, on the 13th of June, 1992, and you said that it was at a crisis staff meeting. Can you explain that, please? Where was the crisis staff meeting held?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And who attended on behalf of the SDA, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, because I didn't know many of these people. I knew one of them. His name was Dizdarevic, but I did not know the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you explain this meeting of a crisis staff in light of part of an order issued by Dario Kordic which this Court already knows about from Z111A, longstanding, from 22nd of May, 1992, which says: "Because the HVO of the Busovaca municipality is leading the whole organisation of life and defence of Busovaca, the Busovaca Municipal Assembly, the Busovaca Executive Council, and the Busovaca Municipal Crisis Command will not do their duties anymore, nor will they make any decisions until the conditions are improved." Now, how does this square with the meeting of the crisis staff which apparently was non-existent at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, we gathered in this crisis staff to discuss the problems in Gradina. We discussed the problem which had arisen in Grablje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you gather there to come to some solution?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we gathered in the municipal building in order to resolve this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But how could there be a decision taken by a nonexistent body? Could you explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know a Serb named Zdravko Bilanovic, or Bilanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where did he live, please? What part of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He lived behind the Catholic church, near the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would that have been an area near Podjele? Would that be a proper area to call it, Podjele?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not Podjele. He had an apartment in the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What happened to him? Where did he go?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where he went. He went over to the Serbian side but I don't know beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That was in May of 1992, was it not, roughly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what year it was. His village, left in November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did it concern you that you were losing members of your Serbian community, which was already rather small?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were concerned but we couldn't do anything about it. It was people's own will, decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You had indicated in one of your summary points that in order to leave Busovaca there had to be written permission. I believe it's number 12. Let me just check. That you had to have -- let's see. Number 12 indicates that you had to obtain HVO passes to be let through checkpoints to travel towards Serb-held territory. Can you tell the Judges, please, from whom you obtained these passes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were obtaining those passes from the HVO, Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. "From the HVO, Mr. Kordic," was that your answer?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, there has been other testimony to this effect, and it was indicated that one Serb who wanted to leave was a fellow named Mico Bulatovic. Do you know him or did you know him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Once you got your pass, how were you able to have safe conduct through to Serb territory? What did the HVO do for you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a convoy would be put together, then the time for departure would be set and we would be given the escort, and the police would go with us until we reached the Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The HVO police?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They had blue uniforms so I think my guess is that it was the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Croat police, in other words.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, such as it was in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you ever make the trip along with any of your fellow Serbs and then return? Have you ever been to Serb territory during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only went as far as Kobiljaca with the convoys, and then I would turn back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That was one end of the road, was that not, the Kobiljaca road, and then there was another ending point. Can you tell us about --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Kobiljaca that was at the end. That was the last Croat checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How long did it take to make the trip?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's some 40 kilometres, and then it depended.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you made the trip, how long did it take you to come and go, from Busovaca to Kobiljaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you, it depended on the size of the convoy and how it could move. So it would take you one hour, an hour and a half, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That was your trip. I'm only asking about your trip. So the convoy was already complete by the time it left Busovaca, or did it pick people up along the way?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The point of departure was Busovaca. That is where people gathered, came from other places to Busovaca, and that was the point of departure. So the convoy did not stop to take up other people from other places, and there were no other people to pick up up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did people leave with their furniture and suitcases full of clothing and other personal possessions? Just what did people leave with, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had only smaller things, their personal belongings, whatever they could put in bags. So I suppose their wardrobe and things like that, nothing of -- nothing bulky.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: These people who left, were they given five minutes to leave, or was this a more timely, planned departure?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their departure was not planned. They were gathering in the municipality of Busovaca, and they were put up in some Serb houses, some Croats also received them. There would be so many of us, not five or ten, but as many that could gather together, we would come together then and the convoy would leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But the Serb families from Busovaca who left, who chose to leave, did they leave in haste or did they have time to gather their things?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not have to leave in haste.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What happened to their furniture, their cars, their apartments? Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cars, they took with themselves, and now the flats are being returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But at that time what happened to those flats? If they were empty, who took them? Were they empty by agreement? What happened to the furniture and other personal belongings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not really know much about that. But those were mostly people who were living in Busovaca who needed flats, who needed housing there, they left it to those friends because most of those flats have survived, they have not been demolished.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How many Muslim refugees were relocated into those Serb houses, if you know, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. All I can tell you is that the village of Katici, which is next to that Muslim village, of 22 houses, three survived. All the others were destroyed. In the town where there were 13 such houses, I believe there are eight still standing. In Kuber, they were all destroyed. In the village of Topolje, they were all destroyed. In Topolje, they were empty but the houses were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you personally resettle any refugees or other persons, including Croat residents of Busovaca, into any of the homes which were abandoned by the retreating Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the town but, yes, in the village where I live now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Whom did you resettle, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are all Croat families accommodated into houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are they still there today?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They came about a month ago to live there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: From where did they come?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One is a refugee family from the municipality of Kakanj, the village of Dusina, and another one from Busovaca municipality, that is, the village of Putis.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I want to make sure I understand. Do you mean from 1992 until a month ago those houses were empty and you just resettled them with refugees from Kakanj and Dusina? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the refugees were going in 1992, they were all in those houses but they were coming and going. They were being accommodated in those houses. After that those houses stayed empty, because these houses are in my village, they belong to my relatives. They were not demolished or anything. And now I was told that there was a need to house some people and I offered these houses for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: They belong to your relatives, does that mean your relatives fled from Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left those houses earlier. One of them was living in Slovenia; another one in Tivat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you know, refugees aside, the particular persons who chose to leave Busovaca on the convoy that you accompanied, where were they actually heading in Serb territory? What was their ultimate destination?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first destination was Rakovica. Then the Serb side distributed them, but I do not know where and how. But the reception centre was at Rakovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure you answered my question about what happened to furniture and possessions. But particularly, what happened to all the livestock of these people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you take any of the possessions or livestock of any of your departing fellow Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you benefit in any way from the sale of any of these items?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To begin with, there was no sale, and I didn't -- secondly, I did not benefit from it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Why did you stay?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that's where I lived, and I didn't want to leave the place where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you didn't have to leave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I did not have to, and I did not leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you explain why all the other people left, if they didn't have to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll explain it to you. The villages that had been left, they were half/half Muslim or were adjoining to Muslim villages, so they left. I mean, they were afraid and that's how they left.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But had they not always been half/half Muslim or adjoining to Muslim villages? What happened that suddenly made them leave?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that, because they were cohabiting with them. How it was, I don't know. What made them leave, I don't know. What was their motive, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were these people who came to you for religious rites or functions in your capacity as the Serbian priest?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did they share with you why they were going or what their particular reasons may have been?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All they said was that they were too afraid to stay there and live, since they were close to the Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But this was 1992. You indicated you had had no problems with the Muslims. Why would they have had a different perspective? What was happening?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in 1992 you already had the incident at Grablje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How many persons were affected, and was there another incident after that in 1992, close in time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after that incident in 1992, all those villagers left. Nobody had left before the incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But you didn't leave. Why? What was different for you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not want to go. Nobody forced me to. I did not live near either of the two groups, because my hamlet stands on its own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, I believe that you have already exhausted this subject, and will you please move on to another issue so that we could make some progress.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about a comment. There was one that was left open by Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And Your Honours, I'm not clear whether the actual paragraph 17 is withdrawn as a point of evidence or how we are looking at these signed statements, but there was no examination elicited on that point. If it, in fact, is withdrawn, I will not ask that question; if it is still pending, or a part of the case, as it were, then I will proceed. Yesterday Mr. Sayers simply indicated that he was not going to ask questions and will leave it to cross, but that was vague as to its status in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said paragraph 17?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, it was 17. And if the position is this is not the -- this does not comprise the entire direct because it is signed, then I will not worry. Otherwise I will ask a brief question about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do not quite understand, Ms. Somers. The point in paragraph 17, you mean paragraph 17 of Mr. Bilic's statement, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And which was the evidence which was to be shown here, which was withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It's unclear what the point would have been; however, the fact that the witness seems to have allegedly under his own hand made that statement, I think should at least bear some inquiry as to why he would come to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 17 says: "I know that several murders were committed in the municipality in early 1993, but I do not know who the perpetrators were. I assume that whichever army controlled a particular territory at the time was responsible for the murders which took place in it." Mr. Sayers, could you please help us on this, on this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Just to remind you of what happened yesterday, we went through this statement in 31 minutes. We wanted to present evidence expeditiously. I just went over that paragraph and said if the Prosecution wanted to ask Mr. Bilic any questions about it, they certainly could. As I understand it, these summaries are not evidence. I think that's pretty clear. They're simply a prediction of what the witness is going to say in Court. And I indicated that he could answer questions addressed to that subject if the Prosecution wanted to ask them. The same convention was used by the Prosecution when they were presenting testimony through their witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Now, if I understand well regarding that paragraph, you are saying this is the exhibit. You did not ask any questions about this item. Is that so? So it is up to you to decide what you want to do about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to get an understanding of what the effect now -- because it is different from our summaries, which were not signed and were simply guidelines.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I will ask you, simply, why on earth you would make the assumption that because something occurred on a particular territory, that an army was responsible for it. What led you to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you had them all over at that time already, so who else could do it but an army?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there no crime at all in Busovaca municipality up to the time of this conflict? Was it a crime-free area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't work for the criminal investigation department to be able to follow the crime rate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You mentioned that a priest in -- let me see now -- in paragraph 14, that there had been several burglaries of a Serb Orthodox priest's apartment. Are you suggesting that those burglaries --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- which were spaced in 1991, and then twice in 1992, were motivated by ethnic factors? Is that your conclusion as a non-police person?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the motive was. The flat was burgled and the perpetrator was found. Whether the motive behind it was just material gain or perhaps something else, or ethnic, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you write this summary that was given to us? Did you sit down yourself and write this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only talked to the lawyer, because I am not competent enough to write that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You mentioned in paragraph 18 your concerns about the crime situation and what you described as armed refugees. It would be the bottom of page 4. Can you explain, please, did you actually witness bands of roving armed women and children coming into Busovaca and committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see gangs of women and children. I saw women and children and men in flight, and in arms and in uniforms, and barefoot and hungry and thirsty, escaping from the Travnik and fleeing from the Travnik municipality to the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And these people were fleeing as a result of having been driven out of their own areas; is that what you're suggesting? You call them refugees.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the result of the conflict between the Croats and Muslims in the Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the number of roadblocks that existed throughout Central Bosnia during the period of time you're discussing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you are suggesting that a person could come from a point from which he was fleeing and not be disarmed by the aggressive powers? Is that what you're suggesting, that the aggressor would not disarm men who were fleeing, or women, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people who were fleeing, they were fleeing under fire, so nobody -- there was no time to do anything. I mean, the fighting was going on and they were retreating. Let me call it a retreat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where was the fighting going on? Be specific. Tell us where and what month and what year, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was June '90 -- I don't remember the year, but it was June and there was fighting around Guca Gora. It was 1993 already; that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Let's talk about 1992. You were mentioning presence of refugees. Where was the fighting at that time? Please specifically tell us where it was coming from, where they were coming from, where there was fighting, and what months they were arriving in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, in November, refugees from Kotor Varos and Jajce arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And did you complain to the police authorities about an increase in the crime rate? Did you file any complaints?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not filing any complaints.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It was your town. Why did you not file complaints? Did you not think it would ultimately affect you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, I didn't really go into town very often, so I would learn something when -- a long time after something had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, I believe that the question of refugees, you have gone through it and --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- will you please be mindful of the time --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the time devoted to the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination, and will you please move on to the next subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour. We just view this particular witness as having information that's terribly relevant to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, please, about the events of January 1993. You told us yesterday that you did not hear the multiple explosions that occurred the night of the 20th of January, 1993, from your not-too-distant home. Can you tell us, please, a little bit about the parade of some 250 or 230 Muslim males up to Kaonik from Busovaca? Did you see that? And that would have been, in fairness, that would have been really the 24th, 25th, and 26th, not the 20th. But from where you were, did you observe that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not observe that. I saw Muslims going from Kaonik to the village Skradno -- no, Strane, and I saw that only once. And what you are saying, I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What were they doing in the village of Strane?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Skradno. To Strane. It's their village. That's where they lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was the date?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did you observe buses or convoys coming and going along the road to Kaonik from where your home was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you indicate, please, if you had been aware during this period of time that Kaonik was being used to detain Muslim males of military age? This would be anywhere from very late 1992 or late 1992 all the way through 1993. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you do anything about assisting any of the Muslims, or any of the other persons, if there were or Serbs, perhaps, in Kaonik, with rations, with food?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To begin with, I didn't know who was there. Yes, I did know some individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Whom did you know who was there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew a man from a neighbouring village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Name, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Asim Sunulapasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know why he was there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you make any effort to inquire?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not inquire why he was in the camp, but later on I started seeing him again outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, the question of Kaonik is not directly related to the direct examination. You were asking questions about Kaonik, and I believe you should now move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The point was more towards his attention or inattention to what was going on in the area, not so much about Kaonik itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Winding down, you mentioned that humanitarian aid, in paragraph 19, was distributed equally, and what did you mean by "equally"?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the food arrived, the number of people was known and it would be distributed. Let's say a hundred tonnes of flour would come, and it would be then divided, distributed, among the number of people who were registered.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In what proportions, do you know? Who set those proportions? Did your group set those proportions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not our group, but it depended on the amount of food that would be brought in, and then based on that, that food would be distributed. Then it would be determined how much would each person get.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And that food was food that came in on convoys guided by UNPROFOR and other members of the International Community; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Let me just check quickly. We probably can end in a second. Did you ever have to seek any permission for any function whatsoever from Anto Sliskovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know who he is or was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him but I don't know what his position was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you know Franjo Sliskovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him. He was a cousin of mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know where he lived by the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know he lived in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know in the apartment of which Serb he was living?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one question, acting Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, the transcript, on page 33, is a little unclear. You said that food was brought in, in a response to a question from Ms. Somers, by UNPROFOR and the International Community. Did you mention any other organisation too that doesn't appear in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I also mentioned Caritas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I thought the translators had missed that but that clears it up. Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Bilic, this concludes your testimony before the International Tribunal. Thank you very much for having come to give your evidence. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness, from the standpoint of cross-examination, will be handled by Mr. Nice who should be on his way to the courtroom now. If the Court would indulge us. If there is any other housekeeping matter that I can assist with, I can try to handle that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me for interrupting. Before starting, my client will need to go to the bathroom in a hurry. Could he leave? I mean, we can work, of course, without him. [Trial Chamber and legal officer confer]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Featherstone has just made a proposal which I will fully endorse. We shall take a break now and we shall be back at ten past eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Maric, wait a moment. You have to take the solemn declaration first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Will you take your seat now, please. Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before we start, I would just like to request something of the Trial Chamber. This is one of the witnesses whose outline is relatively comprehensive and I would like to request that the witness perhaps occasionally consult it, use it as an aide-memoire. He's not going to read from it but just use it occasionally if he needs to remind himself of something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'd much prefer the witnesses not to do that. We've seen quite a lot of witnesses reading their aide-memoires in the Defence case, and I would prefer that not to happen. It's a matter for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that this was introduced, this custom was introduced during the Prosecution case when witnesses were consulting on occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the principle by which we are governed here is that these summaries are not made for witnesses to read them, that they were introduced into our practice to help us move on through testimonies more expeditiously. We shall rather listen to the witnesses directly. It is quite true that there are also some exceptions when we have allowed the witnesses to do it. When you reach a certain point, if there is really a problem, at such point we shall ask Mr. Nice if he insists on his objection on that particular point, and we shall then rule accordingly. So Mr. Naumovski, will you please now begin your examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, would you please state your full name for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, you were born on 6 March 1957, in the village of Podjele, in the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You're an ethnic Croat and you're a Roman Catholic by religion.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You spent your entire life in Busovaca; you continue to live there to date with your wife and two children.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: From my birth until now I have lived in my hometown of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, after you graduated from elementary and high school, you studied forestry in Sarajevo and you graduated in 1982.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, I would just like to ask you to make the work easier for the interpreters, so if you could please pause between my question and your answer.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you have a degree in forestry, and as a forestry engineer you worked in a company in Travnik called Sebesic and then in a company named Lasvansko, and then after that you were part of the Busovaca Forestry Department.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In 1990, when the multiparty system was introduced, you became involved in the formation of the Busovaca branch of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I'm a member of the HDZ from 1 August 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: After the 1990 elections in Busovaca, where the HDZ party received the most votes, you became the president of the municipal parliament.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: At the first session, which was held on 14 December 1990, I was elected the presiding officer, as it was called at that time, and Asim Sunulapasic was also elected there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let us -- when you say that this was a president of the municipal council, or board, that was the local government; isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: After the elections, this municipal assembly worked until the 2nd of April, 1992, when there was a clear threat of war. In this last session of the parliament, to whom did this municipal parliament transfer its powers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: The situation in the territory of former Yugoslavia was worsening, and with the wars in Croatia and Slovenia and with the pull-out of the JNA from Croatia and redeployment of its troops in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the situation was very difficult. And following the principles of the system which was enforced at that time, we needed to call an extraordinary session of the local parliament, which was to appoint a body that would continue to lead the municipality in this situation of the imminent threat of war. In this session I was appointed the president of the crisis staff of the municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand what you said. You were talking about April or another month?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: That was on the 2nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: This crisis staff to which the municipal parliament transferred its powers was composed of members of all parties?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And for the municipality of Busovaca, it meant that it included Serbs, Croats, and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can say openly here that the Croatian Democratic Union and the SDA, which was Muslim, and SDS, which was Serbian, in these first parliamentary elections had a joint list of candidates, and this coalition -- and in addition to this coalition, a list of members, representatives, of the Reform Party and the SDP were also included.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We will later touch on this coalition. I don't want to take you so broadly into this area. But you were the chief of this crisis staff, and from October 1992 until April 1994 you were also acting president of the HVO government in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: After the war ended, from April 1994 until 1996, you were the minister of forestry for Central Bosnia of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Currently, Mr. Maric, you're president of the parliament of the Central Bosnia canton, which is one of the ten cantons in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina established after the Washington Accords?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Currently I am the president of the parliament of the Central Bosnia canton. This canton has a special status, and in the founding session I was appointed the president of this body and I was in that position for about one month. A law was to be put in force where there was to be a rotation between myself and the Muslim representative who was to become the new president, and in November last year I again resumed the position of the president of the parliament of Central Bosnia canton. And in that same session I was also elected a member of the House of Representatives in the Federation, and I'm also a member in the House of Representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which consists of five Croats, five ethnic Muslims, and five Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You said that you were elected at the session of the parliament of Central Bosnia canton, and you received votes from Croats and maybe some others.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: I was elected by all the political parties which were in the parliament. They consisted of the Croats, Bosniak Muslims, and others, and I was elected unanimously.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Just one further detail in that regard. Who is now your deputy? With whom do you rotate in this position of president?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: In the House of Representatives of my canton, it is Ejub Mujic from Kiseljak, an ethnic Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Let me take you to 1990. The Trial Chamber heard enough about the new parties which were formed, nationally based: the HDZ the SDA and the SDS. Now, speaking of the Busovaca branch, the Busovaca branch started organising after the other two ethnic-based parties were already established?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Croatian Democratic Union, in its session of 30th of September, elected its leadership, and I was elected one of them. I was the vice-president. Then Mr. Barac, from Zenica, was elected president.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When you say "30 September," you're referring to 1990?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And who was the other vice-president?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: The other vice-president was Mr. Niko Grubesic, and also Mr. Dragutin Franc, and the secretary -- to the position of secretary, Mr. Dario Kordic was elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When we're talking about this period, you know that Mr. Dragutin Cicak claimed that Mr. Franc was the HDZ president in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: I am not at all surprised that Mr. Dragutin Cicak stated something like this, because he was -- he took an early retirement because of his illness, and Mr. Dragutin Franc was the head of the coalition list for the Busovaca parliament; that is, the coalition of the HDZ, SDA, and SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You mentioned an illness in respect of Mr. Cicak. Were there any problems? You held meetings in your municipal HDZ board. I assume that you attended a number of such meetings where Mr. Cicak was also there. Were there any incidents?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Occasionally there were some when he wanted to push through some of his ideas, but he is a person who is not fully accountable for his actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You touched on something else, and I just want to follow up on this. You said that there were three parties -- the HDZ, the SDA and the SDS -- at the municipal level formed a pre-election coalition where certain things were agreed and a platform was adopted with which you went to elections. Do you know whether the representatives of the SDS, HDZ and the SDA met with the president of SDA, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, in order for him to confirm the -- to the coalition?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Alija Izetbegovic agreed that the SDA should become a coalition member, together with the SDS and the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: My apologies. I think that we are too fast, so I'm pausing, and I would like you to pause also, because it is important that everything said be interpreted. Mr. Maric, the Trial Chamber has had an opportunity to hear that on the 18th of December, 1990, the first parliamentary elections were held in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and your coalition, the coalition of the HDZ, SDA, and SDS, won; they won the largest number of votes in Busovaca municipality. But among the three coalition members, which party won the most?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: At that time the Busovaca parliament had 60 representatives. The HDZ, SDA, and SDS coalition received 64 per cent of the vote. Out of the 64 per cent, the HDZ had 20 representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: On the basis of your pre-election coalition agreement, I assume that you had also agreed on who was going to get which position. Could you just tell to whom some of the top positions were allocated.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: At the first session I was elected the president of the municipality and Mr. Asim Sunulahpasic was elected the president of the local government. According to the list, a Serb was supposed to be given the position of the chief of police. The chief of police was the name used for that position. But the Serbs didn't get that position; rather it went to the Muslims. But Peko Rajak became the secretary of the executive council, that was the third position, and my secretary was Niko Grubesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When you say "they," Peko Rajak was a representative of the Serbs so you're referring to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So who was then appointed the chief of police?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husnija Neslanovic became the chief of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Who was allocated the post of the commander of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: It was another ethnic Muslim. It was Mr. Husein Hadzimejlic who became the commander of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Other positions were also filled in this local government at that time, and one of the positions went to Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kordic was appointed the secretary of the defence, that is, the secretariat of defence as it was called then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The body that you mentioned was part of the civilian government in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumovski, I should only like to ask Mr. Maric if these parties -- that is, the elections in which he participated in 1990, at the beginning of the multiparty system, the three parties he mentioned, the HDZ, the SDA, and SDS, were they all organised on strictly ethnic grounds? Were they all organised on strictly ethnic principles?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: As for the democracy in 1990, which was taking place in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, every people had its own multiparty system, so that the Croat people had the Croat Democratic Union, which was the predominant party in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As for the Party for Democratic Action, it is the party of the Muslim people, which also played an important role in its own people. As for the SDS, it was also one of the important parties of the Serb people. Yes, they were based on the principle of democracy because each one of those parties included the word "democratic" in its name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I just looked at the transcript, Mr. Maric. It doesn't really matter but I believe there is an error, and also in the summary. I said that the first elections took place on the 18th of November. However, here it says December, and also the summary says that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of December I was elected the president of the assembly, that is, the mayor, and Mr. Asim Sunulahpasic, that was when we held the constituting assembly of the municipality of Busovaca. And the elections took place on the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you all know that they took place on the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I do apologise for responding but it was an error and we need to be precise. Very well. Thank you. Then some time in the summer, in July 1991, the JNA offensive began when the Republic of Croatia was attacked. You know which duties Mr. Dario Kordic, as the secretary for the defence of the municipality, discharged in order to prevent young people from joining the JNA and fighting the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. As the situation aggravated in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, from the territory of the municipality of Busovaca, people mostly went to the territories of other republics at the time; that is, those young men who were leaving to serve with the army at that time, Mr. Dario Kordic very actively committed himself, when asked my villagers of other places, to see that their children did not go to the front because the then Yugoslav People's Army would -- as soon as they came to serve the army, they would send them to the front. So their parents were asking that their young sons not be sent from the municipality to serve the Yugoslav People's Army, and Mr. Dario Kordic was helping the people of Busovaca in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Moreover, not only you but other inhabitants in Busovaca, and Mr. Kordic too, of course, conducted certain activities to block the armament convoys going through Bosnia-Herzegovina with a view to preventing that these weapons be taken to the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Well, the weapons were being taken to the territory of the Republic of Croatia, mainly to those areas inhabited by Serbs. So that in October I stopped a convoy heading for Sarajevo, or rather its ultimate destination was Ustikolina, and at that time I stopped that armada at Kaonik. I can also say that that convoy was carrying shells which, at a later stage, began to fall on Sarajevo, and I requested -- I demanded from Mr. Stjepan Kljuic and Mr. Hebib, the then Minister of the Interior, to see what these convoys were transporting in the area. However, this Mr. Hebib, he came and he personally took over and released a convoy which went on to Sarajevo, and lamentably, there the shells were dropping and bombing Sarajevo all that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You have just told the Court about one of the convoys which were coming up. The Court has already had the opportunity to hear about this because a lot has been already said about the village -- about the attack on the village of Ravno. It is paragraph 12. Just one sentence. You will agree, or rather, that is your idea that you, the Croats, perceived the attack on the village of Ravno in September as the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. The first attack, the first armed attack on the -- in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the village of Ravno, was the beginning of the offensive of the JNA on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, some, especially Muslim front men, did not realise that the attack on the village of Ravno was also the beginning of the offensive against the Croat and Bosniak, that is, Muslim, people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, that was the time when young men were leaving, and I'm referring specifically to Central Bosnia, to Busovaca, were leaving to go and help the Republic of Croatia in the defence of its borders. This was not done publicly, was it? It was mostly done on the sly.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Indeed. Many young men went from the territory of the municipality of Busovaca, but not only from the territory of Busovaca, they were going from almost all the territory of the then Lasva Valley, not to say the entire territory where there are Croats, they went to help their brethren in Croatia. When they arrived back in coffins, they had to be buried at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let's just try to give the full portrait of the situation. 1991 is still the time when the only lawful army in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina is still the same JNA, which was attacking the Republic of Croatia. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Quite. The only lawful authority and army, which at that time was then in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are moving to paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In that attack of the JNA on the Republic of Croatia, the shelling of Vukovar, that is, Dubrovnik, added to your concern, distressed further you, the Croats, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm talking about November 1991. Because of what was happening, did you -- and realising the gravity of the moment, did you then try to organise yourselves?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Quite so. The difficult situation in the territories of the former Yugoslavia, and especially if you look at the territories where the Yugoslav People's Army has engaged in an open conflict with Croatia and where thousands of men were getting killed, when there was a major exodus of expelled people, when we could see that this same script was being transferred from the territories of Croatia to the territories of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we then began simply to organise ourselves, to set up a stronger system because we realised -- we saw that the government was looking at it differently and we wanted to organise ourselves in a democratic manner by creating those regions which we tried to unite.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: If I understand you well, at the regional level you simply discussed how to put up a defence against the JNA.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Our principal goal was to defend ourselves against the aggression in the territories of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, the territory of our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In the territory of your region. Was that the Travnik regional community, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Precisely. We first organised ourselves by establishing communication among all the municipalities to see what was the stage of preparedness to resist that aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: However, it was because of the different perception by peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina as to the developments in the Republic of Croatia, you the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina established, how shall I call it, an umbrella organisation, an umbrella union, for you the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Correct. On the 18th of November we organised ourselves in the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You didn't give us the year, sorry. It was 1991, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, sure, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, briefly, in a sentence if you can, which was the primordial task of this Croat Community that was established on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: The Croat Democratic -- that is, the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna its primary goal was to organise itself against the aggression of the Serb army, that is, Yugoslav People's Army at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The Croats were a minority people. This was a minority people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Once again, I mean in percentage terms against other peoples.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: According to the census of 1991, at that time we had about 17.2 or 17.3 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, because it needs to be said at this point in time, until that time, until the beginning of the war, in the territories of the former Yugoslavia, regardless of the numerical size of peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and by this I mean, in the first place, Serbs, Muslims, and Croats, they were all equal constituent peoples of that republic, of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. These three peoples, Muslims came first because they were the largest community, then Serbs, and then Croats; they were constituent peoples in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We are one of the constituent peoples and we wanted to defend our homeland, Bosnia-Herzegovina, on equal terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, you attended the meeting which founded the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna. Mr. Kordic was present too.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was present at that meeting when the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna was founded, and Mr. Dario Kordic was present. He was also the president of the Busovaca HDZ at the time. And we signed it. He signed on behalf of Busovaca. Had he not signed it, then I would have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In those early days, there were not any major activities of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, but as the time went on, the presidency of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna was set up. Will you tell us who became the members? Who constituted the presidency of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, and which were the duties of that body?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: The presidency of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna had its president, and the president was Mr. Mate Boban. The vice-president -- one of the vice-presidents was Mr. Dario Kordic, and also Mr. Bozo Rajic. In addition to these -- along with these bodies we had all the heads, the front men of municipal governments, or rather mayors, mayors from the Croat people and presidents of the executive boards, that is, of local governments from those municipalities which did not have their mayors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So all the municipality's signatories to the declaration were represented on that presidency, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, after July 1991, which was the body in the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna which was responsible for regulator activity, which was a legislative body? Was it this presidency that we are talking about or perhaps some other authority?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: In July 1992, the government was -- of that body was designated; that is, the government which was operated, which was vested with all the properties, qualities of the government; that is, departments for economy, finance, defence, and so on. So, in point of fact, the government was designated. And one of the vice-presidents, one of the deputy prime ministers, was Mr. Jadranko Prlic, and Anto Valenta was the vice-president responsible for Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I see. But let us try to be more precise. So until the appointment of the HVO government, it was the presidency which was responsible for the adoption of laws, was the legislator, and after the government was founded --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: The government took over, assumed all the powers that was necessary for the further functioning of that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
