utterances.text: Yes. There was sporadic gunfire from the Muslim side. There was a quarrel, an altercation, in a village near Kacuni with a predominantly Croat population, and there a kind of a skirmish, I would say, a kind of argument took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you know about an incident when somebody was stopped at Kacuni? In those days, before the 25th of January.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: On the 21st, I believe, of January, Mr. Ignac Kostroman was stopped at the checkpoint at Kacuni and Mr. Ignac Kostroman was threatened, as far as what I know about the whole matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Who is it that told you about that? Who informed you about it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: I received the report from the chief of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In the series of incidents, this was just an additional event which did not improve anything. But in those days, were some premises also damaged in the town of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately these acts of provocation from the Bosnian side reflected on the Croats too who blew up certain premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you know any details about it or were you informed about it as the president of the government, that things like that happened?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received reports from the police that some restaurants and other business premises were blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In your outline you also mention that you had some information about the killing of Mirsad Delija, a citizen of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately that also took place, and this was unfortunately the first victim of these incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Again, you received the police report about it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, and then an investigation was ordered to be launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In your outline you already mentioned the 24 January incident, we can skip that, but we can move on to January 25, 1993. You were at home in the village of Podjele that day.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. That day and until 1998, I continued to live in Podjele. That day I was at home, and at 5.35 a.m. I was awakened by the shelling from the direction -- and the shells were coming from the direction of Merdani and hitting Busovaca. That is when the actual attack started. Then I went from my home to my uncle's home and I spent the day in the shelter. I couldn't get out because from the side of Strane, that is, to the north of where I was, I was the target of snipers, so I could not move and go to Busovaca. So I spent that day at home. On the 26th, in the morning, early, I left Podjele with my wife and two children and we moved to the area of Ravne, which is about 2.5 kilometres south of Busovaca, and I stayed there until June 1994, that is, the end of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: On 26 January, when you came to the outskirts of Busovaca, I assume that you learned what had happened the day before, that there was a conflict, and you received the report of what had happened?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I received the report. There was terrible fighting, that the town of Busovaca was shelled from all sides, that there were casualties. That day, together with Mr. Niko Grubesic, my secretary tried to organise whatever we could to take care of the wounded and others who suffered under the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You also heard whether, on that day, some Muslims were arrested or captured in the town of Busovaca, in the afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I also received a report that those who were able-bodied were taken to Kaonik, to the prison, for security. It was also reported to me that some documents were found which showed that a neighbour -- according to which, some of them were supposed to kill their fellow Croat neighbours, let's say, educated Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumovski, I would like to ask Mr. Maric, because he said that he learned that the 100 Muslims were arrested and taken to Kaonik, Mr. Maric, if you were in charge of the HVO government of the municipality, how come you were not informed about this decision?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: I was in my village; that was at Kaonik. I didn't have a phone line. The war raged on that whole day. I was blocked in my house; I could not leave. Until I arrived in Busovaca, I had no information about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who decided to arrest those people, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: In my view, it was the military, that is, the military side of the HVO which was conducting the operation at the time, so that this was done by the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Didn't the military police depend upon your authority, Mr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: It was under my authority until the beginning of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: A detail, Mr. Maric, just to wrap up this topic. If I understood you correctly, lists of Croats who were to be eliminated were found with certain Muslims.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly what I said. With the Muslims who were with the Territorial Defence, we found documents which testified to the fact that they were tasked with killing Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Who had authority over Kaonik, your government or the military side of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: The Kaonik prison was supposed to be under civilian jurisdiction because it was set up for the common criminals, the perpetrators of common crimes, so to speak. But due to the war situation, it was converted into a military prison because the civilian authorities practically could not operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you're saying that the civilian authorities stopped having jurisdiction over it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. You know that in times of war the military takes over.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I was just waiting for the interpretation. Now, could you tell the Trial Chamber, you had an opportunity to see statistics of those killed and houses and property destroyed. Could you tell us, how many Croats were killed in that conflict, the January conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: I believe it was 50 to 58. There were five women among them; I remember that well. Over 170 Croatian houses were destroyed in the areas of Kacuni, the local commune of Kacuni, Oseliste, Gusti Grab, and outlying areas towards Kiseljak. Obviously there were Bosniak houses which were destroyed in the outlying areas and in Busovaca town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In the outlying areas, you say that about 70 Muslim houses were damaged in the area controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Another detail. Do you know how many Croats were driven out of the territory controlled by the ABiH to the territory controlled by you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: The area of Kacuni and the southern part towards Zenica, that is, Putis, about 250 Croats were expelled from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We will speed up to paragraph 39. After January 1993 an agreement was signed, the hostilities ceased, and you tried to organise everyday life between February and April 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You had an agreement. This was one of the conditions for the signing of the ceasefire agreement after the January conflict: that all the trenches would be covered by both sides.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was an agreement to cover all trenches in Busovaca municipality by both sides, by the HVO and by the TO. However, unfortunately we filled in ours but the Bosniaks kept on digging new ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you also have information how many houses owned by Croats were damaged in parts of Busovaca patrolled by the ABiH during this period between February and April 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: There were quite a few. I think around 180, maybe over 180. I cannot recall right now, but there were a number of damaged properties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We talked quite a bit about crime, and crime continued to increase. There were some murders of Muslims in that period.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, there were some murders too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You knew Ibrahim Hodzic, who was the official with the civilian protection; he worked in that office. And he was killed. Were you able to identify the criminals who had attacked him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: I ordered the inventory of the damaged houses to be produced, and he was a member of this commission. And while this commission was doing its work, he was accosted by some soldiers. He was threatened. And he came to me and he said, "President, what shall I do now?" I said, "Mr. Hodzic, do not go anywhere anymore. Stay away. You see what we have. It's a war. And you see I just received a report that this person's brother was killed." And unfortunately, that same night he was again mistreated, and I then found out that the next day he died from his injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Sir, if it was determined that perpetrators of a certain crime were wearing uniforms, who would have been in charge of an investigation to determine their identity?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: It would have been the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: From this I conclude that the civilian police had no authority over the military personnel.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did the civilian police have enough personnel? Was it fully staffed in 1993 in order to be able to prevent and prosecute criminals?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we did not have enough civilian police officers, nor did we have enough funds to be able to work on crime prevention. These were very difficult times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And the last question on this topic of crime: We agreed that the Muslims were a target of criminals, but also were others, Serbs, Montenegrins and everybody else?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes, and I personally was a victim of these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next topic. This is April 1993. According to you, when did the conflict in April start, in April of 1993, and where in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: The conflict in Busovaca started in Busovaca Kuber, that is, due north, towards Zenica. Then it spread to the east, that is, via Merdani, and then to the north-west, north-east, so that the problems sprang up everywhere and the fighting started everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You said -- what date was this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: It was the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Was it 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Kuber is a very strategic feature?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is strategically a very important feature. It divides Busovaca and Zenica, and actually also Vitez. It separates these three communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you have any ideas about whether fighting was also going on -- how shall I put it? -- along the road towards Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: As I said, it started at Kuber and it went eastward, to the east and south, and north and west, that is, towards Vitez. Because this feature is situated in such a way. It is very prominent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You may have heard in those days that there was also fighting around Ahmici, Santici and other villages along the main road to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Later on I learned that in the areas of Ahmici and alongside the road, there was heavy fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: At that time, after the beginning of April conflict, a large number of Croats left Zenica. What was your estimate as the president of the municipality in Busovaca? How many Zenica Croats had left?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: A large number of Croats left. About 5.000 came to the Busovaca municipality. They were also leaving the Zenica area in the direction of Vitez and Travnik, but they arrived in large numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Those 5.000 of the total number of Zenica Croats arrived in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you know what is the total number of those who left Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Can you tell me, from April 1993 till March 1994, was the town of Busovaca, controlled by the HVO, shelled?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Regrettably, Busovaca was shelled almost constantly. The situation was very difficult. Large Muslim forces were pushing into the Busovaca municipality. The ratio was 10:1. We had only 2.000 able-bodied defenders. And I need to mention that in the course of the combat operations, there were a couple of thousand of Mujahedin who were active, 7.000 Mujahedin who were active in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In respect of the fighting between April and June -- and June is important here because a large number of Travnik refugees arrived in Busovaca -- how many came to Busovaca area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: A significant number of them arrived in Busovaca, and almost every family had to take in another displaced family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: This last large wave of refugees must have added pressure on the local population. Do you remember an order which you co-signed with Mr. Kordic in which you ordered anyone not to disturb property of citizens of Busovaca, regardless of ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. As the president of the municipality of Busovaca, I co-signed an order with Dusko Grubesic, who was the local commander, and Dario Kordic, a person who everybody trusted in the Busovaca municipality, so that we would prevent mistreatment of the Muslim population and expulsion from their homes. We attempted to have people continue to live in Busovaca in the conditions which we all shared at the time, which were very difficult. Unfortunately, with the arrival of these refugees, the situation became very complicated and worsened from day to day. The food stocks were running out, the fuel was running out, and the winter was approaching. There were all kinds of things going on there, and it was very hard on all of us. It is something that you cannot retell; you have to experience it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Naumovski, could you now go on to the next line of questioning, because you need to finish with your direct examination this afternoon. Please, could you do so as to finish this afternoon, before the end of this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best, Your Honour; however, I need to ask one question in respect of the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You personally were also exposed to the -- you had personal contacts with those who were mistreated, and what were these people telling you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: I have to say that I would talk to people, with Croats who were evicting Muslims from their homes. He said, "Sir, I was expelled by Muslims. I have nowhere to go." This was a sad thing. I tried to help, but it was very difficult to do so, because everybody was -- everybody felt threatened, and only those who went through it could understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, let's move on. As the president of the HVO government in -- during most of the period that is pertinent here, you're the right person to ask this question. Did the civilian HVO government or the HDZ in Busovaca, or any other Croat body, conduct a policy of persecution of Muslims in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: It never even crossed our minds, let alone did we persecute and expel other residents from our municipality. We lived in peace. But it is painful to say this. I have to say: We wanted to live together, and today, thank God, we are rebuilding this federation, and I hope we will rebuild it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. As the president of the government and a representative of the civilian government, did you ever receive any order, instruction, advice, from anyone from the civilian or military components of the HVO to persecute Muslims or any other ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: No. I never received such a thing from anyone, because the HDZ and the HVO were not the ones who persecuted anyone, at least not the leadership. We had thousands and thousands of meetings and put in all efforts to keep people there and to avoid the incidents; however, certain extremists did more than we all thought possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You mentioned the ratio of forces and the fact that you defended yourself in Lasva Valley. Perhaps just one fact. In February 1993 you also cared for thousands of refugees who were Muslim, who came from various other areas?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. You should know that we took care of everyone. We shared everything to the last.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I just am pointing to this fact. I am trying -- we are pressed for time. Do you just agree with this fact?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 44, Your Honours, just a couple of questions on Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You have known Dario Kordic since the school days?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have known Mr. Kordic since school days. I am his senior. I went to high school in Travnik and he went to Vitez. We commuted together. I knew him. He was a very correct, a very educated man, who wanted to help everyone, an ambitious man, and he trusted people and people held him in high regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You cooperated with him from 1990 to 1995, when Mr. Kordic went to take another duty in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Kordic was very popular among people, that he achieved a certain reputation, that he excelled, especially when he became involved in the defence, that is, when he tried to prevent the convoys of weapons from leaving for the JNA. That was in late 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, do not lead too much your witness when it comes to the questions about the accused, Mr. Naumovski, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour, I won't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When it comes to the defence against Serbs, you, in Busovaca, in the Lasva Valley, what did you think? What particular hill feature had to be defended in order to defend the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: We were saying that the territory of the municipality of Jajce needs to be defended by Croats and Muslims at all costs, because that was the point. If you want to have a way out, the territories of Kupres, the jugular vein between the Republic of Bosnia with the coast, had been taken over on the sly, and we tried to defend Travnik, the municipality of Travnik, and we did our best to prevent it. But unfortunately, the worst happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When you spoke about Mr. Kordic's role while he worked in the municipal government as the man responsible for national defence, when he prevented young, not only Croats, but also Muslims, from joining the JNA, and parents were so grateful to him, tell us, did that territory, that is, your territory, the territory of the Lasva Valley, did it have to be defended jointly by the Croats and the Muslims, or did Mr. Kordic perhaps have some other idea?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: We were trying, and Mr. Kordic always talked to Bosniak representatives that the concept of defence against the Serbs should be devised jointly. Unfortunately, Jajce fell, conflicts began against Croats too, and then things unfolded as they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Paragraph 46. In 1993, when the war escalated and when Busovaca was surrounded, that is, the whole Lasva Valley, if I may put it that way, what role did Mr. Kordic assume? How did you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic was a politician. He was a politician all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: At that time who did he communicate with on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: In the beginning he communicated with every man, and especially later he communicated with the representatives of the International Community and through them he sought help, insisting that humanitarian relief be brought to this region, to these lands. I say "region." I'm the president of the canton and I always go back to that because my canton spreads from Jajce to Kresevo, 12 municipalities, and that is what I consider "these lands."

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, you also attended a certain number of press conferences; some of them took place in the Busovaca municipal hall where you worked. You heard Mr. Kordic at those press conferences take the floor. What did he speak about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: He informed the public about the developments in the lands of this region.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, have you ever heard Mr. Kordic, in any public or private address, invite violence against Muslims, or any other ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: No. Quite the reverse. He always said we must present a united front and fight for the unity of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I remember that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you ever hear him use derogatory language in addressing another people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: No, never. He always wanted to help everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, you are aware of a protest rally organised by Muslims in Busovaca in late May 1992 in front of the fire brigade centre in Busovaca. At that time you were with Mr. Kordic at a meeting. What was his reaction to that? Was he angry?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: He was not angry at all. We believed that everybody had the right. We are democrats and we wanted everybody to make his protest public.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The Prosecution asserted that Mr. Kordic reacted vehemently, that he wanted to take measures against those people; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Is it true that somebody seized a Muslim flag and committed some outrage upon it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: No, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, to the best of your knowledge and conviction, as the president of the HVO government in those hard times, did Mr. Kordic discharge any military duties? Did you ever hear him issue any military order?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: I said that Mr. Kordic was a politician, and that is what he was throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Today we also spoke about the time when there was no clear distinction drawn between the civilian/military components of the HVO. Tell us, please, following the summer of 1992, who became the military commander throughout the area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Of Herceg-Bosna, that is, throughout the territory of Herceg-Bosna, the commander in chief of all the forces was the president of Herceg-Bosna, that is, Mr. Mate Boban. But as the government was active at that time --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. I wanted to speak about the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. Who was its commander as of 1993 onward?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia was Colonel Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In December 1992, the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade was formed in Busovaca. Who were its commanders, briefly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, its commander, that is, when the brigade was founded, then it was Mr. Ivo Brnada. But the brigade was set up by Mr. Jozinovic and the commander of the brigade was Mr. Dusko Grubesic, and he was succeeded by Mr. Jure Cavara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about Mr. Kordic having supposedly some role in the chain of command of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two brief questions, if I may, Your Honours, and then we shall finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you know that at different times in 1993 telephone lines of Muslims in Busovaca were cut off?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: I must say that in 1993, the system, as I told you before, in the municipality of Busovaca was in the Zenica region; it was under the jurisdiction of the Zenica PTT. So all the lines were blocked, not only those of the Croats -- not only those of the Muslims but of the Croats and the Serbs. All the telephones were cut off. We were under a very heavy blockade and we managed to establish a line to Split. We had a Split number, and that was how we maintained communication with the rest of the world. It was very difficult for us because everybody had to come to my office to talk if he needed to talk to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That is, that line was in your office, was it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Busovaca was not the only place affected by the destruction of telephone lines. Did you hear something about other towns? How did other towns make similar deals with the Croatian post office?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that is how it happened in the municipality of Vitez, and Travnik also established those telephone links. You should also need to know the following: As of the 25th of January, 1993, Busovaca was completely cut off as for the traffic, as for the transportation; that is, no truck, no lorry, could leave the territory of the municipality of Busovaca to go through the territories of other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, we are not experts on telecommunications, and I doubt that you are one, but just to draw the full picture of it. If you had a fax, would that fax, the copy of this fax, show that Split number through which it went?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Split number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In Busovaca, I mean.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Busovaca. "057," if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The last subject, paragraph 50, Mr. Maric. In late March 1993, you received in your Busovaca office, you received Efendi Enver Prolaz, the Busovaca imam.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you remember at whose initiative that was organised?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: Mr. Enver Prolaz, the imam who lived in Busovaca, called me by telephone and asked to see me, and I made it possible for him to come and see me. At first he was quite frightened, he was afraid something might happen to him, but I reassured him and told him, "You can come. Don't worry. Nothing will happen to you." And he came and asked for the permission to leave the territory of the municipality of Busovaca, that is, he and his family. I thought about this man who helped Muslims, Bosniaks, who had stayed behind, whether I should allow him to leave. I thought about it and then I told him, "Mr. Prolaz, yes, you'll be able to leave." I also know about the Prosecutor's allegation that I requested the authority from Mr. Kordic to do that. No. I allowed him to leave and he left. I was the one who let him leave to Zenica, and he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So it was your personal decision and you did not consult anyone about this.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: No, I did not consult anyone. It was a decision that was taken by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would merely like to adduce two more documents. We do not have to comment on them. I only want Mr. Maric to confirm that they are his, and that will be it. They are these last two documents, D273/1 and D274/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, this is the first contract that you signed with UNPROFOR, on a lease of the state, and the second document, of 18 August 1993, is an open letter that you sent to international humanitarian organisations and the domestic and foreign public about the difficult situation in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MARIC
utterances.text: This is one of the letters. I sent it to the entire world, Europe, seeking help, seeking assistance for peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially in those areas where those things were happening, as in our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. There is no need to -- I apologise for cutting in. Thank you, Mr. Maric, for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for your patience. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Naumovski. Let's organise ourselves for tomorrow. I do not know whether you, Mr. Kovacic, would like to cross-examine Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would have some questions of this witness. Not too much, but perhaps 15, 20 minutes maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Now I turn myself to Mr. Nice. How much time do you think that the cross-examination will last?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's hard to tell. It's unlikely to be accommodated within the morning. There's a very great deal of material. Much of it is entirely fresh to me today; a lot of it came fresh at the beginning of the week when we first saw the summary. I think it's highly unlikely I will finish him tomorrow. The Chamber can be heartened by the knowledge that the original timetable, which was only changed, I think, at the beginning of the week or the end of last week, was that he would, in any event, start on Friday and finish on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I only wanted to seek your help. Mr. Maric has been here for the whole week, and I'm afraid -- if perhaps we could work a little longer tomorrow. It would be very difficult for him to stay until Monday because he told us he should get back to his office. We really have a problem there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, my colleague Judge Robinson and myself, we know that Mr. Maric needs to leave because he has got many responsibilities and he should probably not stay here over the weekend. We also do know that you have quite a large number of issues and a large number of questions in cross-examination. So we would like to ask you to do your utmost in order to be able to finish tomorrow with the cross-examination of this witness. When it comes to our schedule, I think that we could continue tomorrow afternoon if need be. Maybe we could work for another hour and a half tomorrow afternoon so that the cross-examination could be completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will do everything I can. I was wrong in saying that he was originally scheduled for Friday and Monday. I think he was originally scheduled for Monday and Tuesday; that was the original plan. I'll do everything I can, of course, to accommodate the Chamber. The Chamber should also have in mind that there are five affidavits allegedly supporting this witness, and of course I have to deal with those as well as with his testimony under the Rules that are applied. But I'll do my best. Can I respectfully remind the Court to warn the witness in the normal way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that there are any problems for the affidavits, and in accordance with our practice, we could leave the affidavits for next week. So we agree that Mr. Kovacic can cross-examine Mr. Maric tomorrow for about 15 to 20 minutes, and then the Prosecutor should organise himself to complete the cross-examination, in which case I think that he would be given exactly the same time as the Defence had which seems to be very fair. So Mr. Maric could leave here before the weekend. Mr. Nice, did you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. I was standing so that you had somebody to address, principally. But what I would add is that I think Your Honour missed my point about the affidavits. The point that is being made by the Defence regularly is that the reason affidavits have to be served before the supported witness gives his evidence is so that cross-examination relating to the affidavits may be put through that witness, and therefore that necessarily may extend the time. Your Honour, all I can say is I will do, of course, my best and I would hope not to detain this witness, or even seek to do so, beyond tomorrow. But I can't know until I see how things unfold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. As far as the affidavits are concerned, I do understand that you should see them in order to see how much you have to cross-examine this witness. And in view of the objections that might be raised, one should be able to ask the authors of these affidavits. In case you can't do it, the Chamber will have to make the final decision. Mr. Maric, as far as you are concerned, you should be back here tomorrow morning at 9.30. I would like to remind you the rule of the Tribunal. I remind you that you are still under oath and that you should not speak with anyone about your statement here. You should not speak with the Defence team either. So you will start again at 9.30 with your cross-examination. We hope that the cross-examination will be completed by the end of tomorrow and that you will be free for the weekend. So now we are going to adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: at 4.25 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday the 2nd day of June, 2000, at 9.30 a.m.
